parts.latex: Prove that $\sec\theta-\cos\theta=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.

solutions.latex:
$$\sec\theta - \cos\theta = \sin\theta\tan\theta$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - \cos\theta \\ &= \dfrac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \\ &= \sin\theta \times \tan\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

A product is zero when one of its factors is zero:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta-1&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta-\cos\theta&=0\\\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta&=0\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Provides significant progress towards the solution, or does not heed the given domain, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\sec^2 A\equiv\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} A}{\operatorname{cosec} A-\sin A}$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\operatorname{cosec}A=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}\\ &=\operatorname{cosec}A\div\left(\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\div\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin A}-\sin A\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\div\dfrac{1-\sin^2A}{\sin A} \end{aligned}$$
Since $\cos^2A+\sin^2A=1$, $\cos^2A=1-\sin^2A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sin A}\times\dfrac{\sin A}{\cos^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2A}\\ &=\sec^2A\\ &=\text{LHS} \end{aligned}$$
Or, using $\sec^2A=1+\tan^2A$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\sec^2A\\ &=1+\tan^2A\\ &=1+\dfrac{\sin^2A}{\cos^2A}\\ &=1+\dfrac{\sin^2A}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2A+\sin^2A}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sin^2A}\\ &=\dfrac{\frac{1}{\sin A}}{\frac{1}{\sin A}-\frac{\sin^2A}{\sin A}}\\ &=\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}A}{\operatorname{cosec}A-\sin A}\\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct manipulation using $\cos^2A=1-\sin^2A$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Determine an expression for $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}$
For what values of $\theta$ is $\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}=0$? Round you answer to three decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, on each term.

For $\dfrac{7}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned}u&=7 & v&=\sin\theta\\ u'&=0 & v'&=\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
For $\dfrac{5}{\cos\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned}u&=5 & v&=\cos\theta\\ u'&=0 & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dL}{d\theta}&=\dfrac{0-7\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{0-5(-\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{-7\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}+\dfrac{5\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates one term correctly while making a major error in the other, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many solutions does $\sec\theta+\tan\theta=0$ have for $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$?

solutions.latex:
Writing $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, for $-\pi\le\theta\le\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}+\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=0\\ 1+\sin\theta&=0,\quad \cos\theta\ne 0\\ \sin\theta&=-1\\ \theta&=-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
But $\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$, so $\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is not allowed.

$\therefore$ There are no solutions.

parts.latex:
Solve the equation $3\sin^2 x+1=4\cos x$ for $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$.

Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Using $\sin^2x=1-\cos^2x$:
$$\begin{aligned}3(1-\cos^2x)+1&=4\cos x\\0&=3\cos^2x+4\cos x-4\\0&=(3\cos x-2)(\cos x+2)\end{aligned}$$
$\cos x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $\cos x=-2$.

$-1\le\cos x\le 1$, so $\cos x\ne -2$ and $\cos x=\dfrac{2}{3}$.

In $[-\pi,\pi]$, $\cos x$ is positive in the first and fourth quadrants:
$$\therefore x\approx\pm 0.841$$

parts.latex:
Which of the following is equivalent to

$$\dfrac{\tan^2x-1}{\tan^2x+1}$$

solutions.latex:
Writing $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, multiplying top and bottom by $\cos^2x$ and using $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\tan^2x-1}{\tan^2x+1}&=\dfrac{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1}{\frac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}+1}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\sin^2x+\cos^2x}\\ &=\sin^2x-\cos^2x\\ &=1-\cos^2x-\cos^2x\\ &=1-2\cos^2x\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and hence evaluate $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is in the fourth quadrant with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, where $\tan$ is negative:
$$\begin{aligned}\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{-\sqrt{3}}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
With $\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (fourth quadrant, related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$):
$$\begin{aligned}\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\times\cot\dfrac{5\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{5\pi}{3}}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} x}{5} - 2 = 0$ for $0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ$, correct to the nearest minute.

parts.latex: Prove that $(1+\sec x+\tan x)(1-\sec x+\tan x)=2\tan x$.

parts.latex: Prove: $\dfrac{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}{\tan x+\sin x}=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x$

solutions.latex:
Method 1: multiply the numerator and denominator by $\sin x\cos x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+\frac{1}{\sin x}}{\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}+\frac{\sin x}{1}}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(\cos x+1)}{\sin^2x+\sin^2x\cos x}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x(1+\cos x)}{\sin^2x(1+\cos x)}\\&=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Method 2: write the numerator using $\cot x=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}+\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin x+\tan x}{\tan x\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\tan x+\sin x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\\&=\cot x\operatorname{cosec}x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct simplification of the compound fraction, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $2\cos^2 x-3\cos x=2$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to a quadratic in $\cos x$ and factorise:
$$\begin{aligned}2\cos^2x-3\cos x-2&=0\\(2\cos x+1)(\cos x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos x=2$.

$\cos x=2$ has no solution, since $-1\le\cos x\le1$.

For $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ the related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Factorises to $\cos x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ (rejecting $\cos x=2$), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve $3\sin x+\sqrt{3}\cos x=0$ over the domain $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and tangent is negative in the 2nd and 4th quadrants:
$$x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

parts.latex:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=2\sec\theta.$$

solutions.latex:
Combine the fractions over the common denominator $\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)$, and use $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta+(1+\sin\theta)^2}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta+1+2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2+2\sin\theta}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{\cos\theta} \\ &=2\sec\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Combines fractions and uses $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \sec\theta\sin^2\theta &&(\text{cancel } 1+\cos^2\theta) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin^2\theta \\ &= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\sin\theta \\ &= \tan\theta\sin\theta \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: $\left(\dfrac{\sin(180^\circ-\theta)}{\sin(90^\circ-\theta)}\right)^2$ can be written as:

parts.latex: Solve $\tan^2 x=3$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$.

parts.latex: If $\sec^2\theta=2$ and $0\le\theta\le\pi$, find all possible values of $\theta$.

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Simplify $\cot\left(270^\circ+x^\circ\right)\cos\left(-x^\circ\right)+\cos\left(90^\circ+x^\circ\right)$

solutions.latex:
Reduce each term using the angle relationships:
$$\begin{aligned}\cot(270^\circ+x)&=\cot\big(360^\circ-(90^\circ-x)\big)=-\cot(90^\circ-x)=-\tan x \\ \cos(-x)&=\cos x \\ \cos(90^\circ+x)&=\cos\big(180^\circ-(90^\circ-x)\big)=-\cos(90^\circ-x)=-\sin x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}-\tan x\cos x-\sin x&=-\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\times\cos x-\sin x \\ &=-\sin x-\sin x \\ &=-2\sin x\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $\left(\cot\theta+\operatorname{cosec}\theta\right)^2=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}$.

solutions.latex:
Write $\cot\theta$ and $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\left(\dfrac{\cos\theta+1}{\sin\theta}\right)^2\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{1-\cos^2\theta} &&\left(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{(1+\cos\theta)^2}{(1-\cos\theta)(1+\cos\theta)} &&(\text{difference of two squares})\\ &=\dfrac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta} &&(\text{cancel }1+\cos\theta)\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Prove that $(\tan x+\cot x-1)(\sin x+\cos x)=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}$

solutions.latex:
Expand the left side, using $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\tan x\sin x+\tan x\cos x+\cot x\sin x+\cot x\cos x-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\sin x+\cos x+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}-\sin x-\cos x\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$
Now the right side, using $\sec x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\dfrac{\sec x}{\operatorname{cosec}^2x}+\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\sec^2x}\\ &=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos x}+\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\sin x}\\ &=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: How many solutions does the equation $(\cos x-1)(2\sin x+1)=0$ for $0\le x\le 2\pi$ have?

solutions.latex:
A product is zero when one of its factors is zero.

$\cos x-1=0$ gives $\cos x=1$, so $x=0$ or $x=2\pi$ (2 solutions).

$2\sin x+1=0$ gives $\sin x=-\dfrac{1}{2}$. The acute angle is $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants:
$$x=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
(2 solutions). The four values are different, so the equation has $4$ solutions.

$$\tan x=\sqrt{3}$$
The acute angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, and $\tan x>0$ in the first and third quadrants.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \text{ or } \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$

Both points lie on $y=\sin x$.

$\therefore A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

$\therefore B\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{1+\tan^2 x}=1-2\sin^2 x$.

solutions.latex:
Use the identity $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$ in the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1-\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\sec^2 x}-\dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sec^2 x}\\&=\cos^2 x-\dfrac{\frac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x}}{\frac{1}{\cos^2 x}}\\&=\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x\\&=\left(1-\sin^2 x\right)-\sin^2 x\\&=1-2\sin^2 x\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Simplifies to $\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Simplify $\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta}$
Hence, solve $\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1-\sin\theta}-\dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta}=1$ for $0\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

solutions.latex:
Combine over the common denominator $(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)$:
$$\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos^2\theta(1+\sin\theta)-\cos^2\theta(1-\sin\theta)}{(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-\cos^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{1-\sin^2\theta} \\ &=\dfrac{2\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &=2\sin\theta \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct combined numerator, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a), the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin\theta &= 1 \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\ln\left(2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta\right)=0$ for $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\ln X=0$ when $X=1$:
$$2\sin^2\theta-\cos\theta=1$$
Using $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2(1-\cos^2\theta)-\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ 2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1 &= 0 \\ (2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

For $0\le\theta\le2\pi$:
$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equivalent to $\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta}$?

solutions.latex:
Use a common denominator, then $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$ and $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1+\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta + 1 - \sin\theta}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= 2\sec^2\theta \\ &= 2\left(1 + \tan^2\theta\right) \\ &= 2 + 2\tan^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
Solve $2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x = 0$, for $x \in [0, 2\pi]$.

Leave your answer in exact form

solutions.latex:
Factorise the left side.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2 x - 5\sin x\cos x + 3\cos^2 x &= 0 \\ (2\sin x - 3\cos x)(\sin x - \cos x) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Case 1: $2\sin x = 3\cos x$, so $\tan x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.
$$x = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) \text{ or } x = \pi + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$$
Case 2: $\sin x = \cos x$, so $\tan x = 1$.
$$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \text{ or } x = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Expresses the equation as a product of its factors, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x}=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x.$

solutions.latex:
Method 1:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{\sin^{2}x}-\dfrac{\sin^{2}x\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\operatorname{cosec}^{2}x-\cos^{2}x \\ &=1+\cot^{2}x-\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right) \\ &=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right)}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\dfrac{1-\sin^{2}x+\sin^{4}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\dfrac{\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{2}x}+\dfrac{\sin^{4}x}{\sin^{2}x} \\ &=\cot^{2}x+\sin^{2}x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct first step (or progress on another method), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find all possible solutions to $\left(\tan^{2}x-1\right)\left(\sin^{2}x-3\cos^{2}x\right)=0$, for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$.

solutions.latex:
A product is zero when one factor is zero, so
$$\tan^{2}x-1=0 \quad \text{or} \quad \sin^{2}x-3\cos^{2}x=0$$
First factor: $\tan x=\pm1$, with acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
Second factor: $\sin^{2}x=3\cos^{2}x$. Here $\cos x=0$ is not a solution, so divide by $\cos^{2}x$:
$$\tan^{2}x=3$$
So $\tan x=\pm\sqrt{3}$, with acute related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
$$x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
Alternatively, using $\cos^{2}x=1-\sin^{2}x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \sin^{2}x-3\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right)&=0 \\ 4\sin^{2}x&=3 \\ \sin x&=\pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
This gives the same solutions.
$$\therefore\ x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \pm\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Solutions from one factor and progress on the other, or equivalent merit
Separates into two factors, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $2\cos x + \sqrt{3} = 0$ in the domain $[0, 2\pi]$

solutions.latex:
Rearrange:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos x+\sqrt{3} &= 0 \\ 2\cos x &= -\sqrt{3} \\ \cos x &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants.

The related acute angle is $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

In the 2nd quadrant, $x=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

In the 3rd quadrant, $x=\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Finds $\cos x=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ or one correct solution, or equivalent merit
